name: Merge Units
subtitle: Merge same-level units to upgrade, leveraging exponential growth for long-term objectives; the core lies in recipes, output curves, and full-cell handling.
demoRuleHint: Rule: Acquire units → Merge same-level units → Upgrade to higher-level units → Increase output → Trigger full-cell handling when a cell is full.
problemsSolved: Transform low-frequency actions into clear long-term goals via merge-and-upgrade.
Maintain continuous pull toward the next level with an exponential growth curve.
Ensure the board remains playable through full-cell or unmergeable handling.
learningGoals: Beginner: understand the minimal loop — feed → same-level merge → level up → higher output — and reproduce one merge and one full-grid handling in the demo
Intermediate: write the full merge-rule contract (same-level judgment, recipe table, full-grid policy) and tune the cost/output curve to control the growth rhythm
Advanced: design pity and anti-farming mechanics, and verify board health with full-grid rate, average merge interval, and tier distribution
minimalRules: Same-level merge rule: at least two units of the same level merge into one unit of level +1; if the target cell is already full after merging, trigger full-cell handling.
Output growth: each unit's output increases with level, starting at 1 for the lowest level and up to 10 for the highest, forming an exponential curve.

Full-cell handling: when a target cell is full and cannot merge, the system alerts and blocks placement; if the player opts to force placement, the system automatically consumes low-level units to free space.
Recipe restriction: same-level merging only applies when the recipe table (e.g., 2→1, 3→1) is satisfied; units not listed in the recipe cannot merge.
systemLoopHint: Input (place/drag) → Evaluation (mergeable?) → Feedback (merge upgrade) → State change (output increase / space release) → New board state → New input.

combos.effect: Offline resource accumulation for merging upon return, reducing daily active pressure.
Exponential output curves amplify growth satisfaction, requiring synchronized consumption design to prevent inflation.
Use level objectives to guide merge direction, preventing aimlessness.

advancedWarnings: A steep output curve can make later levels unattainable, while a shallow curve loses momentum; balancing the exponential growth rate is a core tuning point.
Missing full-cell handling can freeze the board; forcing consumption of low-level units keeps flow but diminishes their value.
High output from low-level units can provide abundant early resources, sometimes more important than high-level units—counterintuitive, so early resource allocation must be considered.
Random drops lacking a safety net amplify frustration; a guarantee and anti-spam mechanism are needed.
advancedAlgoRefs: Merge determination: same-level matching, recipe table, chain merge settlement.
Growth curve: exponential/segmented cost and output design, guarantee and anti-spam.

demoLab.title: Pressure Valve Experiment
demoLab.action: Squeeze "Spawn Interval (pressure valve)" from 6s down to 1s
demoLab.observe: The interval is the board-inflation valve: at 1s, full-grid pressure spikes and you are forced into constant merging; at 6s you get real planning time. Spawn interval sets the thinking budget — the most direct cost-side tuning knob

demoLab.title: Level Cap & Exponential Pull
demoLab.action: Raise "Max Level Cap" from 4 to 7 and compare how long the top tier takes to reach
demoLab.observe: Output grows exponentially per level, so each +1 cap doubles the pull distance to "the next level." Too low and the late game loses its goal; too high and the goal feels unreachable — where you cut the exponential curve decides the game’s lifespan

demoLab.title: Full-Grid Watch
demoLab.action: With a 1s interval and a level cap of 4, refuse to merge until the board jams
demoLab.observe: On a full grid the system warns and blocks placement (or force-consumes low-tier units to free space). Without full-grid handling the board deadlocks — it is the line between minimal rules and a playable product

intro.what: Drag two identical pieces together and they merge into a higher-tier one — 2048, Suika Game, and Merge Dragons are all built on this.
intro.feel: You stack matching pieces and watch them pop into a bigger one; the grid keeps filling up while you juggle space and chase the next tier — simple, but impossible to put down.
intro.why: The pull of exponential growth is nowhere clearer than here — if you want to learn how to give players a long-term goal, merging is the best specimen to dissect.

concept: Merge play is a self-reinforcing growth engine: same-level merging converts low-frequency actions into deterministic tier jumps, and an exponential output curve keeps "the next tier" forever more valuable than "this one." The hard part is not the merge rule — it is three loop-closing details: a full grid must always have an escape that never deadlocks, the feed rhythm must leave a thinking budget, and the level cap decides how far the pull reaches. The "just one more merge" addiction comes from the curve shape, not the art.
designNotes: The pull comes from the exponential curve, not the reward count: doubling output per tier means the next tier is always worth chasing — but too steep and the late game feels unreachable, too flat and the goal dilutes. Where you cap the curve is the switch for the game’s lifespan.

Low-tier units are worth more than high-tier ones (counterintuitive): early output rides on a broad base of cheap units, and rushing tiers starves your own production — good merge design lets players discover "build the base first, then climb" on their own.

A full grid is not a punishment; it is a pacing valve: force-consuming low-tier units to free space looks like a penalty but is actually the fuse that prevents board deadlock — it turns "space management" from a background rule into an explicit every-move decision.
